newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-GERMAN F.A. DENIES OFFER TO CO-HOST FINALS WITH ENGLAND.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GERMAN F.A. DENIES OFFER TO CO-HOST FINALS WITH ENGLAND.

text.p: The German soccer federation (DFB) denied on Monday that its president Egidius Braun had offered in a television interview to share staging the 2006 World Cup finals with England.
Michael Novak, spokesman for the DFB, said that Braun had said nothing about sharing during an interview with ARD television on Sunday night.
A report circulated in the British media on Monday that Braun had made such an offer.
"We are unaware of any such comment having been made by Egidius Braun," Novak said. "We saw the interview and he did not make any such comment."
Adding he believed the report may have been the result of a journalist misunderstanding Braun, Novak said he wanted to make further checks that Braun had not made the comments anywhere else.
The German soccer squad left for Israel earlier on Monday for a friendly match in Tel Aviv on Wednesday.
Alec McGivan, the director of England's bid to stage the 2006 World Cup finals, had reacted coolly to the report on Monday.

McGivan said on BBC Radio: "If our colleagues at the German FA come to us with some form of proposals or plan, we would have the courtesy to discuss it with them. I don't think we can say no to anything straight away. But we have a very strong bid on our own which can stand up on its own. For us, the only option under consideration is our own bid and that is not going to change in the near future."

Two weeks ago McGivan told Reuters that the possibility of England and Germany co-hosting the finals was slight, explaining: "I'm sure that if the bids from England and Germany were so strong that no one could choose between them then it might be a possibility. But so much would have to happen before that ever became a reality I can't see it materialising."

Other countries besides England and Germany are also expected to bid for the finals in nine years time, including Australia, South Africa, Morocco and a possible joint-venture from Argentina and Brazil.

McGivan said on Monday: "There's quite a debate going on about whether this tournament will be in Europe or not. The South Americans feel they have a strong case to make as well, so we shouldn't assume this tournament will be in Europe although tradition would have it that it probably will be."
Both Germany and England are to push their individual claims when UEFA's Executive Committee meets in Geneva on April 17.
UEFA will only back one bid, and a public row blew up earlier this month when it appeared that UEFA had given their backing to Germany without any prior consultation.
That situation changed following a protest from the English F.A. who believe their hand has been strengthened by growing animosity towards a possible German bid from German pressure groups.
